points: Jumping converts the speed of the run-up into height (high jump) or horizontal distance (long and triple jump) at take-off.
The distance or height achieved depends on the take-off speed, the take-off angle and the height of the centre of mass at take-off.
Take-off uses a powerful, extended drive of the hip, knee and ankle, and the free leg and arms swing upward to add lift.
Newton's third law explains take-off: the jumper pushes down into the ground, and the ground reaction force pushes the jumper up and forward.
Run-up: a curved, J-shaped approach, straight at first and then curving in the final strides.
Run-up: the jumper leans away from the bar on the curve.
Take-off: the jumper takes off from the foot further from the bar, driving the knee of the free leg up.
Take-off: the body rotates so that the back faces the bar.
Flight: the jumper arches over the bar with the head and shoulders back and the hips high, then lifts the legs over.
Landing: the jumper lands on the upper back and shoulders on the mat.
Run-up: an accelerating run-up with a consistent number of strides, checked by a check mark on the runway.
Take-off: an active, flat-footed take-off from the board, without stopping on the board.
Take-off: the free knee is driven up to help the body rotate forward.
Flight: the jumper uses a hang, a sail or a hitch-kick to keep balance and delay the legs dropping.
Landing: the legs are extended forward, and the jumper falls forward or sideways, not backwards.
Run-up: as for the long jump, with an accelerating run-up and a consistent stride pattern.
Take-off (hop): the jumper takes off from the board and lands on the same foot.
Flight (step): the jumper lands on the other foot, keeping the phases balanced.
Landing (jump): the jumper lands in the pit on both feet.
The sequence is always hop, then step, then jump.
The phases should have roughly even rhythm, and speed is maintained through all three.
Landings are active and flat-footed.
Arm action, either single or double, drives each phase.

notes.h: Rules and fouls for jumping events
points: High jump: the take-off must be from one foot.
High jump: three consecutive failures eliminate the jumper, whether at one height or across heights.
High jump: the bar must stay on the supports; knocking it off is a failure.
Long and triple jump: stepping over the take-off board line is a foul.
Long and triple jump: the jump is measured from the take-off line to the nearest mark in the sand made by any part of the body.
An efficient jump has a consistent run-up, speed maintained through take-off, an upright posture at take-off and a controlled landing.
Slowing down before the board removes the speed that the jump depends on.
Overstriding at take-off lands the foot ahead of the body, which brakes the jump.
Sitting back on landing loses distance.
Flattening the curve in the high jump reduces the lean away from the bar and the rotation needed to clear it.
Landing pits are dug and raked before any jump.
Landing mats are positioned and checked before the high jump.
The runway is clear of people and equipment during the run-up.
Spikes are checked for damage before use.
The take-off area is dry, so the jumper does not slip at take-off.

keyTerms.definition: The final push from the ground that launches the jumper into flight, using a powerful extension of the hip, knee and ankle.
The point at which the body's mass is balanced; its height and angle at take-off determine the jump.
The high jump style in which the jumper takes off from the foot further from the bar and clears it back first.
A long jump flight technique in which the legs are cycled to delay them dropping and keep the body balanced.
The first phase of the triple jump, in which the jumper takes off and lands on the same foot.
The second phase of the triple jump, in which the jumper lands on the other foot.
A mark on the runway that a long or triple jumper uses to check that the run-up has the right number of strides.
The board from which the long and triple jumper takes off, over which the jumper must not step.

factCards.term: Triple jump: the order of the phases
factCards.definition: Hop (takes off and lands on the same foot), then step (lands on the other foot), then jump (lands in the pit on both feet).

factCards.term: High jump: which foot to take off from
factCards.definition: The foot further from the bar.
Three consecutive failures eliminate the jumper, whether at one height or across heights.
A hang, a sail or a hitch-kick, used to keep balance and delay the legs dropping.

factCards.term: Long and triple jump: how the jump is measured
factCards.definition: From the take-off line to the nearest mark in the sand made by any part of the body.

questions.prompt: Describe the run-up, take-off, flight and landing in the long jump, giving key technique points for each phase.
questions.model: Run-up: the jumper accelerates with a consistent number of strides, checked by a check mark on the runway, so the foot lands on the board at the right point. Take-off: the jumper makes an active, flat-footed take-off from the board without stopping, driving the free knee up to help rotation and keeping the body upright. Flight: the jumper uses a hang, a sail or a hitch-kick to keep balance and delay the legs dropping, so that the legs can be extended further forward. Landing: the legs are extended forward and the jumper falls forward or sideways, not backwards, so that the mark in the sand is as far from the take-off line as possible.

questions.prompt: Describe the three phases of the triple jump.
questions.model: The triple jump has three phases in a fixed order. The hop is the first phase: the jumper takes off from the board and lands on the same foot. The step is the second phase: the jumper lands on the other foot, keeping the phases balanced and maintaining speed. The jump is the third phase: the jumper lands in the pit on both feet. Arm action, either single or double, drives each phase.
